# The canonical grammar

**What this is.** The assistant's meaning space is CANONICAL ENGLISH generated by a grammar over the vault ontology (Overnight-style semantic parsing). Every canonical utterance is a tree; every node maps deterministically to a parameterised read fragment or a typed vault command. Nested reads come from recursion: a relative clause is a filter, a link walk is a join-or-sequence, an aggregate is a wrapper. A model's only job, later, is PARAPHRASE — user text to canonical — and multi-turn is a rewrite of the previous canonical.

**What this is not.** It is not a description of the eval suite. The terminals are derived from the ontology (§2) and the grammar was written against them; the suite was then MAPPED onto it and the places where a suite turn forced an addition are recorded as such in [COVERAGE.md](COVERAGE.md), because that is signal about the ontology rather than licence to special-case a corpus.

**The artefacts.** [`map.json`](map.json) is every turn of `suite.json` and `blind.json` with its canonical and its parse; [`check.py`](check.py) is the parser, and it is the same parser that GENERATED every `tree` in the map, so the map cannot drift from the grammar. Run `python3 check.py`. [`derive/`](derive/README.md) takes the terminals out of the ontology mechanically, generates both parsers' tables from them, and writes [`DIFF.md`](DIFF.md) — the derived grammar against this one.

---

## 1. The grammar

Literals are `"quoted"`; dates are bare (`2026-06-19`, `2026-06-19T14:00`, `2026-05`, `2026-06-04..2026-06-06`). A `Set` operand is parenthesised wherever it is nested; a `Pred` is always parenthesised.

```
Turn    := "show" Set                       -- a list of rows
         | "same?" Set Set                  -- IDENTITY between two sets (§1.1)
         | Value                            -- a number, or one field
         | Cmd                              -- a typed write
         | Cmd ("then" Cmd)+                -- an ORDERED SEQUENCE of writes
         | "nothing"                        -- the member withdrew
         | "refuse" ":" Reason               -- outside the vault at all
         | "clarify" ":" Reason              -- (reserved; normally EMITTED, §4)

Value   := "count" "of" Set
         | ("sum" | "min" | "max") Field "of" Set
         | Field "of" Set                   -- field projection
         | "balance" "of" Set "in" Set      -- the Tally reader (§2.5)

Cmd     := Verb "{" Args "}" [ "on" Set ]
Args    := ( Name ":" ArgVal ) *
ArgVal  := Lit | Date | "null" | "true" | "false" | "me" | Duration
         | "(" Set ")"                      -- an id resolved from a set
         | Value                            -- e.g. `due_at: dtstart of (it)`

Set     := Kind                             -- a board
         | Kind "of" Set                    -- LINK WALK (§2.3)
         | Set "called" Lit                 -- label match
         | Set "that" "(" Pred ")"          -- relative clause
         | Set "during" Window
         | Set "ordered by" Field ("asc"|"desc")
         | Set "and" Set                    -- union
         | Set "except" Set                 -- difference
         | "first" Num "of" Set             -- limit
         | Ref                              -- context terminal (§3)

Pred    := Pred ("and"|"or") Pred | "not" Pred | "(" Pred ")"
         | Field Cmp (Lit | Num | Date | "true"|"false"|"null"|"me"
                      | Field                 -- FIELD-TO-FIELD (§2.4)
                      | "(" Set ")")          -- an id from a nested set
         | Field "contains" Lit
         | Field "in" "(" Lit ("," Lit)* ")"
         | Field "during" Window
         | Field "around" Num                 -- BAND (§2.4)
         | "count" "of" Kind Cmp Num          -- COUNT OVER THE WALK (§2.4)
         | Field "is" ["not"] ("null" | "me")
         | "member of" Set                    -- membership via a link table
Cmp     := "=" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">="

Window  := "today" | "tomorrow" | "yesterday" | "before now"
         | "this week" | "last week" | "next week"
         | "this weekend" | "last weekend"
         | "this month" | "last month"
         | "next" Num ("days"|"weeks"|"months")
         | Date | Month | DateRange
         | "from" "(" Value ")" "to" "(" Value ")"   -- ANCHORED (§2.6)

Ref     := "it" | "them" | "that one" | "the N'th one" | "the other one"
         | "the earlier one" | "the last thing I added"
```

**`and` and `except` bind LOOSER than the postfix operators.** `photos called "Ana" and photos called "Marco"` is the union of two NAMED sets, not a named union; a postfix over a union is written with the union parenthesised, which the rule above ("a `Set` operand is parenthesised wherever it is nested") already requires. `check.py` and `crates/candidates/src/canon.rs` implement the same precedence, and the round-trip test is what keeps them one grammar. Before 2026-09-21 both bound `called` to the whole union, which silently made `s118.1` ("have I got a photo of any of them?") mean ONE photo instead of two — DEFECTS #34.

### 1.1 `same?` — the identity question

```
Turn := "same?" Set Set
```

**Both operands are `set_primary_or_group`**, so each is either a single primary (a `Kind`, a `Ref`, a `walk`, a `first N of …`) or a PARENTHESISED `Set`. A postfix chain written bare — `same? members called "Neha" …` — does not parse and must be written `same? (members called "Neha") (…)`; without the parentheses there is no way to tell where the first operand ends and the second begins. Both parsers agree on this and `s31.1` is written that way.

Executed as an **id-set intersection**: `yes` when the two sets share a row, `no` when both resolve and share none, and — under the executor's R-C4 — `clarify` when they are sets of UNRELATED KINDS, which is the case the addition exists for.

`s31.1` is that case. "Is that the same Neha as my dinner on tuesday?" puts a Tally **member** beside the **parties** an Agenda event names, and the vault holds no relation between the two: a Tally friend is its own `core_party`, and an event that says "Dinner with Neha" in its summary names nobody. An empty intersection there is not evidence of difference — it is evidence the vault cannot tell, and answering `no` would be inventing the one fact the question asked for. So the rule is stated in the grammar rather than left to the executor to stumble into:

> **An intersection over sets of unrelated kinds is `clarify`, never `no`.** Two sets are of unrelated kinds when no `Link` (§2.3) joins their entities. Where a link does exist, an empty intersection is a real `no`.

Writing the turn as `show (parties of (it))` was considered and rejected: it maps a different question — it asks who, and the member asked whether.

### 1.2 `Cmd then Cmd` — the ordered sequence

```
Turn := Cmd ("then" Cmd)+
```

One sentence, two writes, and the arguments differ. `s107.3` ("that one needs to be thursday; it's the booking that goes to friday") moves two rows to two different days; `s113.3` rolls one expense back and trashes another; `h61.0` finishes a task and cancels the event of the same title. A `Cmd` carries one Verb and one `Args`, and a `write_set` reaches these only when ONE verb with ONE argument applies to a union of rows (`s75`), so none of the three could be said at all before.

`then` and not `and`: the order is part of the meaning (`s113.3` must restore before it trashes, or the member's own correction reads as two trashes), and `and` is already the union inside a `Set`. The executor runs the steps in the sentence's order and **the first step that declines is the turn's outcome** — a half-finished sequence is worse than none, for the same reason a bulk write is all-or-nothing (R-W1).

### Depth bounds

`Set` recursion is bounded at **4** and `Value` may wrap it once, so a legal tree is at most **5 constructors deep** and holds at most **2 link walks**, **4 filters** and **2 aggregate wrappers**. Those are not aesthetic caps: they are the observed ceiling over 199 canonicals plus one step of headroom, and they are what makes the meaning space ENUMERABLE for a retrieval-style runtime. The realised distribution is in [COVERAGE.md](COVERAGE.md) §4.

## 2. Deriving the terminals

Every terminal below is a projection of a file in the repository. The source is named for each, so a change in the ontology is a change in the grammar.

### How the terminals are derived

This section used to be a HAND transcription of the ontology, and §2.7's "175 `CommandDefinition`s" is what that costs: the registry holds **148**, and the other 27 were entity-type strings a regex could not tell apart from command names. A prose table cannot notice that. So the terminals are now GENERATED, and this section describes the generator rather than standing in for it.

`derive/derive_grammar.py` walks the ontology and writes `derive/derived.json` — the terminal set the vault can support, with nothing in it a human chose:

| source | form | what is taken from it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `contracts/schema/vault-ddl.sql` | SQLite DDL, generated from the golden vault's `sqlite_master` | columns, declared types, `CHECK (col IN (…))` value sets, foreign keys, primary keys |
| `contracts/schema/v0-registries.json` | JSON | entities (logical name, table, lifecycle, `projectionOf`), sealed columns |
| `crates/apps/*/manifest.json` | JSON, one per door | each door's declared READ scopes — which entity it may hand back |
| `crates/search/src/domains.rs` | Rust | the seven FTS domains and their label columns |
| `crates/vault/src/commands/*.rs` | Rust | the 148 `CommandDefinition`s: name, input schema, gates, handler SQL |

A **Kind** is an (entity, door) pair the door's manifest grants a read scope over; a **Link** is a foreign key read either way; a **predicate family** is the column's declared shape; an **Agg** is a numeric or date column; a **Verb** is a registry entry, and a verb **CLASS** is the set of commands whose handler SQL has one effect — every command that stamps `deleted_at` is a `delete`, which is how `core.trash_document`, `schedule.delete_task` and `locker.trash_item` group without anybody listing them.

`derive/terminals.json` supplies the one thing the ontology cannot: the WORDS. The vault holds `core.event`, never "events". It also carries the terminals of the CONVERSATION — `Ref`, the window phrases, the decline reasons — which are not the vault's to say. `derive/emit.py` validates every name in it against the derivation (a Kind the doors do not serve, or a class member that is not a registered command, is refused) and generates BOTH parsers' tables from the pair: `grammar/lexicon.py` for `check.py` and `crates/candidates/src/canon_terminals.rs` for `canon.rs`. `python3 check.py` re-runs the generator and fails when either committed file is stale.

**The productions stay hand-written in both.** A production is the shape of the meaning space and the ontology has nothing to say about it; only terminals are generated. `canon.rs` used to describe its lexicons as "transcribed from `grammar/check.py`", and a transcription is the thing that drifts — the `and`/`called` precedence bug (DEFECTS #34) was that failure one level up.

[`DIFF.md`](DIFF.md) is the derived set diffed against the written one, in three sections: what the ontology supports and the grammar lacks, what the grammar claims and the vault cannot serve, and what differs only in spelling. It names the turns each item touches.

### 2.1 `Kind` — from the entity registry × the app doors

`contracts/schema/v0-registries.json` `entities[]`, every entry whose `lifecycle` is not `machinery` (63 of 96), intersected with the eight app doors. The name is the plural a member would use; the mapping is to `(logical entity, door)`:

| Kind | entity | door | base table |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `events` | `core.event` | agenda | `core_event` |
| `tasks` | `schedule.task` | tasks | `schedule_task` |
| `notes` | `knowledge.note` | notes | `knowledge_note` |
| `journal notes` | `knowledge.note` | **people** | `knowledge_note` |
| `documents` | `core.document` | docs | `core_document` |
| `parties` | `core.party` | people | `core_party` |
| `members` | `core.party` | **tally** | `core_party` via `tally_friend` |
| `profiles` | `people.profile` | people | `people_profile` |
| `important dates` | `people.important_date` | people | `people_important_date` |
| `contact channels` | `social.contact_channel` | people | `social_contact_channel` |
| `activities` | `core.activity` | people | `core_activity` |
| `obligations` | `tally.obligation` | people | `tally_obligation` |
| `photos` | `core.content_item` | photos | `core_content_item`+`media_asset` |
| `albums` | `media.album` | photos | `core_collection` |
| `notebooks` | `knowledge.notebook` | **notes** | `core_collection` |
| `places` | `core.place` | photos | `core_place` |
| `expenses` | `tally.expense` | tally | `tally_expense` |
| `groups` | `tally.group` | tally | `tally_group` |
| `circles` | `social.circle` | tally | `social_circle` |
| `settlements` | `tally.settlement` | tally | `tally_settlement` |
| `accounts` | `core.account` | tally | `core_account` |
| `transactions` | `core.transaction` | tally | `core_transaction` |
| `projects` | `schedule.project` | tasks | `schedule_project` |
| `locker items` | `locker.item` | locker | `locker_item` |
| `things` | `*` | all eight | — (§4, R-T1) |

**Not every (entity, door) the doors serve is a Kind.** The manifests grant 119 read pairs and a member never names most of them: a door reads `core_link` so it can render a backlink, not so anyone can ask for their links. So every read scope in `crates/apps/*/manifest.json` DECLARES a `surface` —

- `kind` — a member names it and asks for the board. The 24 rows above.
- `facet` — a row that only exists inside a parent kind, reached only as `X of (Kind …)` and never as a bare board: `locker.item_field`, `tally.expense_line_item`, `schedule.section`, `core.party_identifier`, `schedule.calendar`, `tally.recurring_expense`.
- `internal` — the other 88: edges (`core.link`, `core.tag`, `core.attachment`, `core.collection_entry`, `knowledge.annotation`), revisions, representations, and every entity a door joins through rather than shows.

`derive/derive_grammar.py` computes each pair's DEFAULT from the ontology — trashable or a search domain is a `kind`; a polymorphic `(X_type, X_id)` pair is an `internal` edge; a NOT NULL `ON DELETE CASCADE` (or registry `owned-child`) parent plus a label of its own is a `facet`; a command's `writes` naming it is a `kind`; and a `kind` is only a `kind` at its HOME doors, the ones that can mint one. A manifest may override the default and must then say why in `surfaceReason`. `emit.py` holds the two sides together BOTH ways: a Kind above whose scope is not declared `kind` is refused, and a scope declared `kind` with no Kind named for it is refused. `DIFF.md` carries the split and every override.

**A Kind is (entity, door), not entity alone.** `journal notes` and `notes` are the same entity behind two doors that return different rows — the People journal is a `knowledge.note` the Notes library does not hand back — and `members` and `parties` are the same table reached through two rosters whose rows do not correspond. Collapsing either pair loses an answer the vault actually holds. This is the single largest thing the ontology says that a naive "one entity, one board" grammar would not.

**Locker is a Kind and is not a search domain.** `crates/search/src/domains.rs` has seven domains and Locker is structurally absent ("a secret cannot become a link target by adding a probe"). So `locker items` compiles to the Locker app's own shelf read and never to the FTS plane, and `things` (§4 R-T1) fans out over the eight doors rather than over the seven domains.

### 2.2 `Field` — from the base tables, minus the sealed set

Physical columns of the Kind's base table in `contracts/schema/vault-ddl.sql`, minus `v0-registries.json` `sealedColumns` for that table. A sealed column may appear only under `is null` / `is not null`: presence is not plaintext, and `crates/apps/kit/src/grammar.rs` enforces exactly that split at the door, so the canonical grammar inherits it rather than restating it.

On top of the columns, the facts an app's own READER computes and hands back beside the row are Fields too — `status`, `effort_min`, `favorite`, `starred`, `folder`, `album_titles`, `owed_to_them`, `role`, `cadence_days`, `next_occurrence`. These are derived from each app crate's reader (the `extra` bag `crates/evalsuite`'s doors already carry), not invented here; a grammar that only knew columns could not express "which pictures did I favourite".

### 2.3 `Link` — from the foreign keys, not from a second list

`Kind_b "of" Set_a` is legal exactly when the DDL relates them, in either direction:

- **down an FK** — `tally_expense.group_id → tally_group` gives `groups of (expenses ...)` (b28);
- **up an FK** — the same edge read the other way gives `expenses of (groups ...)`;
- **through a join table** — `tally_expense_split`, `core_collection_entry`, `media_memory_member` give `photos of (albums ...)`;
- **self-referential** — `schedule_task.parent_task_id` gives `tasks of (tasks called "Plan the Tahoe trip")` (s27, b10);
- **through `core_link`** — the generic relation, when a `relation_concept_id` exists between the two entity types.

Direction is INFERRED from the ontology, not written, because one FK is one relation and spelling the direction would let a canonical claim an edge twice. **When no edge exists the walk does not parse-to-execute — it clarifies** (R-C4). That rule is what keeps the assistant from inventing a link: s50.2 asks whether there is an event at a photograph's place and the honest answer is that nothing relates `core_place` to `core_event`.

### 2.4 `Pred` — from each column's declared shape

| column shape | predicate forms |
| --- | --- |
| `TEXT` label column (a search domain's `labels`) | `called`, `contains` |
| `TEXT` with a `CHECK (col IN (...))` | `=`, `!=`, `in (...)` over exactly the CHECK's values |
| date/instant `TEXT` | `during Window`, `<`, `>`, `is null` |
| `INTEGER` | `=`, `<`, `>`, **`around Num`** |
| nullable anything | `is null`, `is not null` |
| two columns of the same type on one row | `Field Cmp Field` |
| a join table | `member of Set` |
| an FK pointing AT this row's table | **`count of Kind Cmp Num`** |

Two of these are worth stating out loud.

**`around` is a BAND, not an equality and not a budget.** A member who says "about a forty five minute job" is naming a magnitude. The band is `[centre/1.5, centre*1.5]` — half again either way — clipped to the column's granularity. On `effort_min` around 45 that is `[30, 60]`, which is the one estimate of 15/45/120 the member meant. A grammar with only `<=` would read the same phrase as "under 45 minutes" and answer with two rows.

**`count of Kind` is a count over the WALK, taken from the row being filtered.** "Which of these places have I got exactly two photos from?" (`s112.1`) is `places that (count of photos = 2)`: the edge is the ontology's (§2.3), read backwards, and the count is over the rows that walk reaches from THIS row. Stating it as a predicate rather than as an aggregate operand is what keeps the grammar free of a correlated-reference terminal — there is nothing for the inner set to refer to, because the walk's source IS the row.

**`Field Cmp Field` is how a derived state is said without a derived column.** "Which logins have I never rotated the password on" is `password_set_at = created_at`: the vault records the rotation stamp and the creation stamp and never a `rotated` flag, so the predicate is the ontology's own answer to the question.

### 2.5 `Agg` — from the numeric columns, plus one app reader

`count` over any Set; `sum`/`min`/`max` over any numeric or date Field; `Field "of" Set` for the projection of a single column (`cadence_days of (profiles of ...)` — a cadence is a column, not a statistic).

`balance of Set in Set` is the ONE aggregate that is not a fold over one table: it is `crates/apps/tally/src/balance.rs::group_net`, a signed fold over `tally_expense_payer`, `tally_expense_split` and `tally_settlement`. It is a terminal because the app owns the arithmetic — a grammar that re-derived it would be a second definition of what somebody owes, and the two would disagree the first time a settlement landed.

### 2.6 `Window` — from `crates/evalsuite/src/reference.rs::calendar`

The named/vague split is the corpus's published convention and the grammar reads it rather than restating it: **a named period is a calendar period, a vague one is a rolling window**, both inclusive and compared on the date part. `before now` is the overdue comparison. `next N months` is forward from today.

`from (Value) to (Value)` is the ANCHORED window: its ends are values the vault itself holds. "While we're at the cabin" is `from (dtstart of (events called "check-in")) to (dtstart of (events called "check-out"))` — a window the member's own diary draws, and the only form that survives the trip being moved.

`next_occurrence` is the derived date Field on `people_important_date`, which stores `month_day` and not a date. Without it, "any birthdays this month" has no column to compare against.

### 2.7 `Verb` — from the typed command registry

The **148** `CommandDefinition`s in `crates/vault/src/commands/*.rs`, by name — the nine `definitions()` listings, not every quoted `schema.name` string in those files. (Until 2026-09-21 the lexicon scraped the latter and admitted 175 terminals, 27 of which were entity types such as `core.event` and `locker.item` rather than commands. No canonical used one; the count in this sentence was wrong for as long as the scrape was.) A canonical never writes SQL and never names a table in a `Cmd`; the Args are the command's own JSON schema, and the executor fills in what the schema requires and the canonical does not carry (the default split on `tally.add_expense`, the calendar id on `schedule.propose_event`, the sealed cell and the minted id on `locker.add_item`).

**Verb CLASSES.** `reschedule`, `delete`, `restore`, `complete` and `cancel` are classes, not commands: they resolve to `schedule.edit_task` or `schedule.reschedule_event`, to `knowledge.delete_note` or `core.trash_document` or `locker.trash_item`, once the anchor's Kind is known. They are derived by grouping the registry on (effect, subject kind).

| class        | effect the handler SQL has  | members                     |
| ------------ | --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `reschedule` | sets `dtstart` or `due_at`  | 2                           |
| `delete`     | stamps `deleted_at`         | 8                           |
| `restore`    | clears `deleted_at`         | 8                           |
| `complete`   | stamps `completed_at`       | 1 (`people.complete_task`)  |
| `cancel`     | sets `status = 'cancelled'` | 1 (`schedule.cancel_event`) |

`restore`, `complete` and `cancel` fall out of the same grouping as the first two and were missing from this section until 2026-09-22 — the derivation found them, which is what a derivation is for. `complete` has one member because `schedule.set_task_status` writes a status rather than the stamp, and `cancel` has one because an event is the only thing in this vault with a `cancelled` status. The class is necessary because a member says "push the cabin booking to Friday" BEFORE anyone knows whether the cabin booking is a task or an event — and in this vault it is both. Without the class the parser would have to guess a command to state the meaning, which is exactly the guess the clarify rule exists to prevent.

---

## 3. Multi-turn: a rewrite of the previous canonical

A session holds the previous canonical and the rows its execution answered. Five moves, and every follow-up in both corpora is one of them:

| move | what changes | example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `substitute` | one terminal is replaced, the shape is kept | s06.1 `notes called "Tahoe"` → `notes called "Emerald Bay"` |
| `refine` | a clause is ADDED to the previous Set, over the ROWS it answered | s01.1 `show (them that (dtstart during this weekend))` |
| `act` | a `Cmd` or `Value` is wrapped around the previous ANSWER | s60.1 `core.star_document{} on (it)` |
| `undo` | the request is withdrawn; nothing runs | s09.1 `nothing` |
| `new` | the thread is dropped and a fresh canonical begins | s51.1 |

The `Ref` terminals are what make a rewrite a TREE and not a string edit:

- `it` / `them` — the rows the last **list** answered.
- `the N'th one` — by position in an `ordered by` answer; an ordinal into an unordered answer clarifies.
- `the other one` — the complement inside a two-row answer.
- `the earlier one` — the answer TWO turns back. Forced by s15.2: "what else is in there" is the album's frames minus the photograph named two turns ago, and `it` by then is the album.
- `the last thing I added` — the row the last `Cmd` created.

**R-X2, the transparency rule.** A `Value` turn does not replace the held rows. After `who do I owe money to` / `how much?` / `pay it off`, `it` in the third turn is still the party from the first — the middle turn asked a number about those rows, it did not change what "it" means. Without this rule s53 and b18 lose their last turn.

---

## 4. The executor

One node, one fragment. A `Set` compiles to a read against its Kind's door; a `Cmd` compiles to `Vault::execute(name, args)`.

**Recursion does NOT compile to a subquery.** `crates/apps/kit/src/grammar.rs` — the door's own statement grammar — refuses subqueries by construction: a statement is tables and equijoins, a select and a where, and nothing else. So a nested `Set` compiles to a SEQUENCE: the inner set is read first, its ids are collected, and the outer read binds them with `kit::reads::in_list`, walking pages with `read_pages` when the set is bounded by a window rather than by a table. A grammar that emitted nested SELECTs would be refused at the door. This is the single biggest constraint the repository puts on the design and it is the reason the depth bound in §1 is a budget on ROUND TRIPS, not on SQL.

Per-node fragments:

| node | fragment |
| --- | --- |
| `Kind` | the door's board read for that (entity, door), `deleted_at IS NULL` |
| `Kind of Set` | inner ids → `WHERE <fk> IN (?,…)`, or the join table's two-step |
| `called Lit` | `WHERE lower(<label col>) LIKE lower('%' |  | ? |  | '%')` — the FTS domain when the Kind has one, the board scan when it does not |
| `that (Pred)` | the `Pred` fragment, `AND`-ed |
| `during Window` | `WHERE substr(<salient date>,1,10) BETWEEN ? AND ?` |
| `ordered by F d` | `ORDER BY F ASC\|DESC` |
| `and` / `except` | id-set union / difference in code, after both reads |
| `first N of` | `LIMIT N` after the order |
| `Ref` | the held ids, bound as an `in_list` |
| `count` / `sum F` | `COUNT(*)` / `SUM(F)` over the compiled set |
| `F of Set` | project `F`; the set must resolve to exactly 1 row |
| `balance` | `tally::balance::group_net`, then index by party |
| `Cmd` | one `execute` per anchor row, in the anchor's order |

**R-W1 — the anchor rule.** A `Cmd` with an `on` clause runs once per anchor row. One row is the ordinary write; several rows is a bulk write, and a bulk write is ALL-OR-NOTHING (half of it is worse than none, because the member believes it finished). Zero rows is R-N1.

**R-W2 — per-row Args binding.** Inside `Args`, `it` is the anchor row currently being written, not the held set. `amount_minor: balance of (it) in (groups called "Tahoe Trip")` therefore pays each member their own balance. Without this, "settle up with everyone in the group" is one instruction whose three outcomes cannot be stated.

**R-W3 — sealing is the executor's, not the canonical's.** `locker.add_item` refuses plaintext by name, so the executor mints the item id, asks the seat to seal the cell against it and passes the ciphertext and the key id. A canonical that carried a sealed value would be a canonical that had already leaked.

**R-T1 — the top kind.** `things` is the union over all eight doors. As a `show` it is a legitimate list (s16, b11). As a `Value` or a `Cmd` anchor it is NOT: see R-C2, R-C3.

**R-T2 — `things during Window`** is `events ∪ open tasks ∪ important dates`. A member asking "what's on Wednesday" means the calendar and the board and the birthday that is on neither, and a completed task is not "on".

### Clarify, refuse, nothing

`clarify` and `refuse` are EMITTED by the executor. Three of the rules below fire on facts the executor learns at run time, which is the point: the parse says what was meant, the execution says whether the vault can honour it.

| rule | condition | outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **R-C1** | a `Cmd`'s anchor, or a `Value`'s set, resolves to ≠ 1 row where 1 is required | clarify |
| **R-C2** | a `Value` over `things` resolves across more than one Kind | clarify |
| **R-C3** | a destructive verb class over an anchor that spans Kinds, or over `things` | clarify |
| **R-C4** | a link walk whose edge the ontology does not hold | clarify — never infer the edge |
| **R-C5** | a `Ref` with nothing in the session to resolve it | clarify |
| **R-R1** | the verb is outside the command registry (transact on a website, fetch weather) | refuse |
| **R-R2** | the effect moves sealed material out of custody (send a password, bulk-export the locker) | refuse |
| **R-R3** | a required literal is a secret the member did not supply | refuse — never fabricate |
| **R-R4** | a destructive verb over an UNBOUNDED set (no `called`, no `that`, no window) | refuse |
| **R-N1** | a `Cmd` whose anchor resolves to 0 live rows while a trashed row matches | nothing |
| **R-N2** | the Turn is `nothing` (the member withdrew) | nothing |

**R-C3 against R-R4 is the whole difference between "delete all my dentist stuff" and "delete every note in the vault".** The first is SCOPED and ambiguous — nine rows across seven apps — and the member should be asked which. The second is UNSCOPED, and there is nothing to ask: the answer is no.

**R-N1 is a third declination and not a polite clarify.** "Delete the note about the old clinic" when that note is already in the trash has nothing to do and nothing to ask; saying so and doing nothing is the whole correct outcome, and a runtime that clarified would be offering to delete the LIVE dentist note.

---

## 5. Conventions the corpus follows

Every rule here is a reading the grammar left open and the corpus had to settle one way. Three were **ruled by the owner on 2026-09-21** (C1–C3); the rest (C4–C12) are clarifications of rules already in §3 and §4, written down because the executor was already behaving one way and the grammar did not say so. Each names the turns that depend on it.

### The owner's rulings, 2026-09-21

**C1 — "due" means OPEN.** A `what's due …`-shaped turn carries `status != "completed"` beside its window. A completed task is not due; it is done. Applied to `b02.1`, `b06.0`, `b07.0`, `b55.0`, which had the window and not the predicate. The obligation-side spellings of the same idea (`settled_at is null` on `outstanding …`) already carried it. No expected id changed: no completed task in either world falls inside any of those windows, which is what made the omission survive unnoticed.

**C2 — a referent's NUMBER follows the rows written.** After a `Cmd`, `it` where one row was written and `them` where several were. Applied to `s86.1`, `s88.1`, `s89.1`, `s90.1`, each of which said `them` about a single restored row. `s111.4` ("what's left of them?") keeps `them`: its antecedent is the two-row LIST the session read, not the one row it ticked off, and the member's own sentence says so.

**C3 — "what's on `<weekday>`" is `things`, not `events`.** A member asking what is on a day means the calendar, the board and the birthday that is on neither — which is exactly R-T2, and R-T2 is the reason the Kind is `things`. `s58.0` moved from `events during tomorrow` to `things during tomorrow`; its expected ids are unchanged because that Tuesday carries no open task and no important date.

### Clarifications

**C4 — an ordinal indexes the answer AS DELIVERED.** §3 says an ordinal into an unordered answer clarifies. Every answer this executor gives has an order — the door's own, or an explicit `ordered by` — so the ordinal indexes the order the member was shown. `s111.3` ticks "the first one" off a filtered list with no sort of its own, and there is nothing else it could mean. (`s18.1`, `s49.1`, `s107.2`, `h37.1`.)

**C5 — R-C1 counts ANSWERS, not rows.** One row is needed where the answer would otherwise be ambiguous; several rows that all hold the same value are not ambiguous. "How often am I supposed to call Ray" over nine Rays who share a cadence has one answer and not a question.

**C6 — where the rows DISAGREE, the door's rank resolves.** `called` is a ranked retrieval against the FTS plane, and the plane's own order is the only resolution the product has. Dropping it would make "Ray" a coin toss, which is worse than a wrong answer because it is a different wrong answer each time. C5 and C6 together are what R-C1 means in a vault with collisions.

**C7 — `things` includes the obligations.** R-T1 is the union over the eight doors, and a debt is one of the things a member has about the dentist even though no board row holds it: the People reader hangs it off the party. So the fan-out joins the obligations the roster computed. (`s03`, `s35`, `h42`.)

**C8 — an empty walk out of rows the session HOLDS is a clarify.** §1.1 makes an intersection over unrelated kinds a clarify; the same reasoning covers a walk that reaches nothing from rows the member is looking at. "Which Neha is that?" over a dinner whose summary names nobody is the vault being unable to tell, and an empty list would assert the one fact the question asked for. R-C4 stays what it was — an edge the ONTOLOGY does not hold — and this is the run-time half of it.

**C9 — a row that NAMES a party stands for that party.** The vault holds no edge from a phone number to a diary, and it holds both edges through the person, so "and when am I seeing her?" after "what's her number?" is one hop each way. This is not an inferred edge: both legs are real foreign keys. Over several source rows the bridge takes the parties COMMON to all of them. (`s110.3`, `h65.5`.)

**C10 — a topic backtrack retries the earlier answers.** §3 has five moves and none of them is "the member came back to what we were talking about two turns ago". An empty answer over a `Ref` is the signal — a member who says "those two" is not asking about nothing — so `it`/`them` is retried one answer further back, up to two. (`s114.3`, `s115.4`, `s120.1`.)

**C11 — R-X2, read the other way.** A `Value` turn does not REPLACE the held rows; it does not follow that a session which has only ever asked for numbers holds none. Where the first turn folded a set and nothing else has been read, the rows it folded are what a refinement refers to. (`b21`.)

**C12 — `it` narrows to the row just written.** Where the held answer is a list and the session has just written to one row of it, "star it" means that row: the member is still talking about the thing they moved, not about the list they read on the way past. `them` is the plural and never narrows. (`s60.1`, `s108.3`, `s115.2`.)

**C13 — `the earlier one` has ONE sense: the ANSWER two turns back.** §3 says so and `s15.2` and `s112.4` use it that way. Where the antecedent is instead the row a previous SENTENCE named — `h68.3`, "and the rest of that spot's frames?", where the frame to exclude is the one the previous question picked out and not the answer it got — the canonical NAMES it (`except (photos called "Fog over")`). A second terminal for "the row named two turns back" was considered and rejected: it would make the session state carry a per-turn SUBJECT beside its answers, for one turn, and the grammar can already say the thing exactly.

**C14 — a pronoun whose antecedent the SENTENCE supplied is resolved in the canonical.** A `Ref` reaches into the conversation's ANSWERS. Where the antecedent is a row the member themselves named a turn or two earlier, the §3 rewrite resolves it and the canonical carries the name. `s117.4` ("log that I called him about it today") follows "and Ray?", whose answer was a number, so `him` has no held rows to point at and the canonical says `parties called "Ray Alvarez"`; `s92.1` ("how much does she still owe me?") follows a diary read naming Ana Ferreira and the canonical says so. A `Ref` is kept wherever the antecedent really is the previous ANSWER — `s90.1` ("no, put her back") and `s110.2`/`s110.3` are all deixis into a result and stay as they are.
